Linear algebra is the study of vectors, of the linear equations that tie them together, and of the maps that preserve their structure. It is the working language of numerical computing, statistics, machine learning, graphics, quantum mechanics and control, and it is the first course where most students meet mathematics built from definitions and proofs rather than from formulas. This six-post series is written for a reader who knows high-school algebra and wants the full senior-undergraduate picture: computation first, then the abstract theory, with proofs of the key theorems. Post 00 starts at the very beginning — vectors in Rn, linear combinations, span, the dot product, systems of linear equations and Gaussian elimination — and ends with the structure of a solution set and a first look at linear independence. Posts 01–05 cover matrix algebra and LU, vector spaces and dimension, linear maps and determinants, eigenvalues, and inner products through the spectral theorem and the SVD. The standard textbooks behind the series are Strang (computation and the four subspaces), Lay (clear worked examples), Axler (the abstract, determinant-free view) and Hoffman–Kunze (the classical rigorous treatment).
Series map: 00 Vectors & Linear Systems (this post) → 01 Matrix Algebra, Inverses & LU → 02 Vector Spaces, Basis & Dimension → 03 Linear Maps, Change of Basis & Determinants → 04 Eigenvalues & Diagonalization → 05 Inner Products, Spectral Theorem & SVD.

Add and scale vectors in Rn, and describe a linear combination both algebraically and geometrically.

Compute dot products, lengths and angles, and recognise orthogonal vectors.
Read a system Ax=b in two ways: the row picture (intersecting lines or planes) and the column picture (a combination of columns).
Apply the three elementary row operations and explain why they never change the solution set.

Prove that a solution set is "one particular solution plus all homogeneous solutions".
Test a small set of vectors for linear independence.

Symbol · Meaning
R, Rn · real numbers; column vectors with n real entries
x,v,b · vectors (bold lower case), always columns unless stated
xi · the i-th entry of x
A,B,U · matrices (capital letters); aij is the entry in row i, column j
m×n · m rows, n columns
aj · column j of A
AT · transpose (rows become columns)

Scalar — a single real number. Later in the series scalars may come from any field (see Linear Algebra 02), but for now they are real.
Vector in Rn — an ordered list of n real numbers, written as a column. The numbers are its entries or components.
Zero vector 0 — the vector whose entries are all 0.
Vector addition — add entry by entry. Only defined for two vectors of the same length.
Scalar multiplication — multiply every entry by the same scalar.
v=(v1v2⋮vn),v+w=(v1+w1⋮vn+wn),c v=(cv1⋮cvn).

For all u,v,w∈Rn and all scalars c,d:
u+v=v+u and (u+v)+w=u+(v+w).
v+0=v and v+(−v)=0.
c(u+v)=cu+cv and (c+d)v=cv+dv.
c(dv)=(cd)v and 1v=v.
Each rule follows from the matching rule for real numbers, applied one entry at a time. These eight rules are exactly the axioms of a vector space; Linear Algebra 02 turns them into a definition, and then polynomials, functions and matrices become "vectors" too.

In R2 and R3 a vector is an arrow from the origin to the point with those coordinates.
Addition is the parallelogram rule: place the tail of w at the head of v; the sum ends where w ends.
Scaling stretches the arrow by ∣c∣ and reverses it when c<0.
v−w is the arrow from the head of w to the head of v.
For n>3 there is no picture, but every algebraic fact still holds. The habit to build is: reason with the algebra, check the intuition in R2 or R3.
Watch out: a point and a vector are written the same way in Rn, but they play different roles. A point is a location; a vector is a displacement. The distinction matters in Chapter 7, where a solution set can be a plane that does not pass through the origin.

Linear combination of v1,…,vk — any vector c1v1+c2v2+⋯+ckvk with scalars c1,…,ck (the weights or coefficients).
Span — the set of all linear combinations:
span⁡{v1,…,vk}={ c1v1+⋯+ckvk:c1,…,ck∈R }.
The span always contains 0 (take every weight 0) and each vi itself (weight 1 on it, 0 elsewhere).

Vectors · Span
only 0 · the single point {0}
one nonzero v · the line through the origin in direction v
two vectors, neither a multiple of the other · the plane through the origin containing both
two vectors, one a multiple of the other · still only a line
three vectors not in one plane · all of R3
three vectors in one plane · only that plane (or a line)
The pattern "adding a vector enlarges the span only if the new vector is not already inside it" is the seed of linear independence (Chapter 8) and of dimension (Linear Algebra 02).

Is b=(1,5) a combination of a1=(2,1) and a2=(−1,1)? We need x,y with
x(21)+y(−11)=(15)⟺2x−y=1x+y=5.
Adding the two equations gives 3x=6, so x=2 and y=3. Check: 2(2,1)+3(−1,1)=(4−3, 2+3)=(1,5). So b is in the span. In fact, since a1 and a2 are not parallel, their span is the whole plane R2.
The key lesson: "is b in the span of these vectors?" is the same question as "does this linear system have a solution?" Everything in this post comes back to that sentence.
This chapter is brief; inner products get their full treatment in Linear Algebra 05.

Dot product: u⋅v=u1v1+u2v2+⋯+unvn. It takes two vectors and returns a scalar.
Length (norm): ∥v∥=v⋅v=v12+⋯+vn2.
Unit vector: a vector of length 1. For v≠0, the vector v/∥v∥ is the unit vector in the same direction.
Orthogonal: u and v are orthogonal (perpendicular) when u⋅v=0.

The dot product is symmetric (u⋅v=v⋅u), linear in each argument, and positive definite: v⋅v≥0, with equality only for v=0. Two inequalities hold for all u,v∈Rn (proofs in Linear Algebra 05):
∣u⋅v∣≤∥u∥ ∥v∥(Cauchy–Schwarz),∥u+v∥≤∥u∥+∥v∥(triangle inequality).
Cauchy–Schwarz is what makes the angle formula legitimate: for nonzero vectors the ratio below lies in [−1,1], so it is the cosine of exactly one angle θ∈[0,π].
cos⁡θ=u⋅v∥u∥ ∥v∥.

Let u=(1,2,2) and v=(2,−2,1). Then ∥u∥=1+4+4=3, so u/3=(1/3,2/3,2/3) is a unit vector. And u⋅v=2−4+2=0, so u and v are orthogonal.
Trick: the dot product gives a second reading of one equation. The equation a1x1+⋯+anxn=b says a⋅x=b. When b=0, the solutions are exactly the vectors orthogonal to a — a line in R2, a plane in R3, a "hyperplane" in general.

Linear equation in x1,…,xn — an equation a1x1+⋯+anxn=b with constant coefficients ai and constant b. No products xixj, no powers, no sin⁡x.
System of linear equations — a finite list of linear equations in the same unknowns.
Solution — a vector x that satisfies every equation at once. The solution set is the set of all solutions.
Consistent — has at least one solution. Inconsistent — has none.
Equivalent systems — systems with the same solution set.
Coefficient matrix A — the m×n array of the aij. Augmented matrix [ A∣b ] — A with b attached as an extra column.

Write the columns of A as a1,…,an. The product Ax is defined as a combination of the columns, with the entries of x as weights:
Ax=(a1a2⋯an)(x1⋮xn)=x1a1+x2a2+⋯+xnan.
Entry i of that combination is ai1x1+⋯+ainxn, which is the dot product of row i of A with x. So there are two ways to compute Ax — by columns and by rows — and they always agree. A system of m equations in n unknowns is therefore one vector equation Ax=b, with A of size m×n, x∈Rn and b∈Rm.
Two rules follow straight from the definition and are used constantly: A(u+v)=Au+Av and A(cu)=c Au.

Take the system from Chapter 2:
2x−y=1x+y=5⟺(2−111)(xy)=(15).
Row picture. Each equation is a line in the xy-plane: y=2x−1 and y=5−x. A solution is a point on both lines. They cross at (2,3).
Column picture. The same system asks for weights on the columns (2,1) and (−1,1) that produce (1,5). The answer is 2 of the first column plus 3 of the second.
The same numbers x=2, y=3 appear in both pictures, but they mean different things: a point where lines cross, or weights in a combination.
In R3 the row picture has three planes, and a solution is a point common to all three. The column picture has three column vectors in R3, and the question is whether b is a combination of them. The column picture scales to any size and becomes the main point of view from Linear Algebra 02 onwards (column space).

Theorem (zero, one or infinitely many). A linear system has either no solution, exactly one solution, or infinitely many solutions.
Proof. Suppose x and y are two different solutions, so Ax=Ay=b. For every real t, put zt=x+t(y−x). Then
Azt=Ax+t(Ay−Ax)=b+t(b−b)=b.
Since y−x≠0, different values of t give different vectors zt, so there are infinitely many solutions. ■
Geometrically: the whole line through two solutions consists of solutions. Two lines in the plane cannot meet in exactly two points.

Three operations on the rows of an augmented matrix:
Replacement — add a multiple of one row to another row: Ri←Ri+cRj (with i≠j).
Interchange — swap two rows: Ri↔Rj.
Scaling — multiply a row by a nonzero constant: Ri←cRi, c≠0.
Two matrices are row equivalent if one can be turned into the other by a finite sequence of these operations.
Theorem. If two augmented matrices are row equivalent, the corresponding systems have the same solution set.
Proof. It is enough to check one operation at a time. Any x that satisfies the old equations also satisfies the new ones: a swap or a scaling changes nothing essential, and if x satisfies equations i and j it satisfies their sum "i+c⋅j". Conversely, each operation can be undone by an operation of the same type — replacement by Ri←Ri−cRj, interchange by the same swap, scaling by 1/c (this is why c≠0 is required). So any solution of the new system also solves the old one. ■
Common pitfall: multiplying a row by 0 is not allowed. It destroys an equation and can create new "solutions". Scaling needs c≠0 precisely so the step is reversible.

x+2y+z=23x+8y+z=124y+z=2[ A∣b ]=(1212381120412).
Step 1 — clear column 1 below the first pivot. The first pivot is the 1 in position (1,1). Row 2 needs multiplier ℓ21=3/1=3; row 3 already has a 0, so ℓ31=0.
R2←R2−3R1:(121202−260412).
Step 2 — clear column 2 below the second pivot. The second pivot is 2 in position (2,2). Multiplier ℓ32=4/2=2.
R3←R3−2R2:(121202−26005−10).
The coefficient part is now upper triangular, with pivots 1,2,5.
Step 3 — back substitution. From the bottom up: 5z=−10 gives z=−2. Then 2y−2z=6 gives 2y=2, so y=1. Then x+2y+z=2 gives x=2−2+2=2.
Check in the original equations: 2+2−2=2, 6+8−2=12, 4−2=2. The unique solution is (x,y,z)=(2,1,−2).
The multipliers 3,0,2 are not thrown away in practice — Linear Algebra 01 stores them in a lower triangular matrix L and gets the factorization A=LU.

Zero in a pivot position, nonzero below it — swap rows and continue. This is a temporary breakdown.
Zero in a pivot position and zeros all the way down — there is no pivot in that column. The matrix is singular (Linear Algebra 01) and the system has either no solution or infinitely many. Chapter 6 handles this case completely.
Watch out: on a computer, a pivot that is merely small is as dangerous as a zero one, because dividing by it magnifies rounding error. Software therefore swaps in the largest available entry of the column (partial pivoting). By hand, with exact numbers, any nonzero pivot is fine.

Leading entry of a row — its leftmost nonzero entry.
Row echelon form (REF) — (i) all zero rows are at the bottom; (ii) each leading entry is in a column to the right of the leading entry of the row above; (iii) all entries below a leading entry are zero.
Reduced row echelon form (RREF) — REF, plus (iv) every leading entry is 1, and (v) each leading 1 is the only nonzero entry in its column.
Pivot position — a position that holds a leading entry in an echelon form of the matrix. Pivot column — a column containing a pivot position.
Basic variable — a variable whose column is a pivot column. Free variable — any other variable.
Gauss–Jordan elimination continues past REF: scale each pivot to 1, then clear the entries above each pivot, working from the bottom pivot up.

Theorem. Each matrix is row equivalent to one and only one matrix in reduced row echelon form.
Existence is the Gauss–Jordan algorithm. Uniqueness takes a careful induction on the number of columns; see Lay, Appendix A, or Hoffman–Kunze, Chapter 1. It has an important consequence: the pivot positions — and so the pivot columns, the number of pivots and the split into basic and free variables — do not depend on which row operations you chose. An REF is not unique (you can always scale a row by 2), but its pivot positions are.

Solve Ax=b with
A=(1222246836810),b=(167).
Forward elimination, R2←R2−2R1 and R3←R3−3R1:
(122210024400244).
Column 2 has no pivot (zeros from row 2 down), so move to column 3; its pivot is the 2 in row 2. Then R3←R3−R2:
(122210024400000)(REF).
Gauss–Jordan: R2←12R2, then R1←R1−2R2:
(120−2−30012200000)(RREF).
Pivot columns are 1 and 3, so x1,x3 are basic and x2,x4 are free. The RREF reads
x1=−3−2x2+2x4,x3=2−2x4,x2,x4 free.

Write the free variables as parameters x2=s, x4=t and collect terms:
x=(x1x2x3x4)=(−3020)+s(−2100)+t(20−21),s,t∈R.
The solution set is a 2-dimensional plane inside R4, one parameter per free variable. Check the first vector: A(−3,0,2,0)=(−3+4, −6+12, −9+16)=(1,6,7)=b.

The zero row of the augmented RREF above ended in 0, so it said 0=0 — harmless. Change b to (1,6,8) and the same steps end with the row (0 0 0 0∣1), which says 0=1. That system is inconsistent. In general:
Theorem (existence and uniqueness). A linear system is consistent if and only if the last column of its augmented matrix is not a pivot column — that is, no echelon form has a row (0 ⋯ 0∣c) with c≠0. If it is consistent, then it has exactly one solution when there are no free variables, and infinitely many when there is at least one free variable.
Proof. Row operations do not change the solution set, so study the RREF. A row (0⋯0∣c) with c≠0 is the equation 0=c, which nothing satisfies. If there is no such row, every nonzero row of the RREF has a leading 1 in a coefficient column and expresses one basic variable in terms of the free ones; choosing any values for the free variables produces a solution. With no free variables that solution is forced and unique; with at least one free variable each choice of its value gives a different solution. ■
For b=(b1,b2,b3) and our A, the condition works out to b3=b1+b2: row 3 of A is row 1 plus row 2, so the right-hand sides must obey the same relation.
Trick: count before you compute. If A is m×n and has r pivots, then r≤m and r≤n, and there are n−r free variables. Here m=3, n=4, r=2: two free variables, and a solution for b only when b passes one test (one zero row).

Homogeneous system — Ax=0. It always has the trivial solution x=0.
Nontrivial solution — a solution x≠0.
Theorem. A homogeneous system with more unknowns than equations (n>m) has a nontrivial solution.
Proof. There are at most m pivots, one per row, so at least n−m>0 variables are free. The system is consistent (it has 0), so by the existence-and-uniqueness theorem it has infinitely many solutions, and in particular a nonzero one. ■
For the 3×4 matrix above, Ax=0 has the same RREF with a zero last column, and its solutions are
x=s(−2100)+t(20−21).
The two vectors are the special solutions: set one free variable to 1, the others to 0, and solve. This set is a plane through the origin — the null space of A, studied in Linear Algebra 02.

Theorem. Suppose Axp=b. Then the solution set of Ax=b is exactly
{ xp+xh:Axh=0 }.
Proof. If Axh=0 then A(xp+xh)=b+0=b. Conversely, if Ax=b, put xh=x−xp; then Axh=b−b=0 and x=xp+xh. ■
Compare with the parametric form in Chapter 6: (−3,0,2,0) is a particular solution, and the s and t terms are exactly the homogeneous solutions. Geometrically, the solution set of Ax=b is the null-space plane shifted by xp — parallel to it, but not through the origin (unless b=0).
Common pitfall: the solution set of Ax=b with b≠0 is not closed under addition: if Ax=Ay=b then A(x+y)=2b. Only the homogeneous solution set is a "subspace". The particular solution is not unique either — any solution can play that role.
This is the same structure as linear differential equations ("general solution = particular solution + solution of the homogeneous equation"), and for the same reason: the operator is linear.

Linearly independent — vectors v1,…,vk such that the only solution of c1v1+⋯+ckvk=0 is c1=⋯=ck=0.
Linearly dependent — not independent: some combination with not all weights zero gives 0. Such an equation is a linear dependence relation.
Put the vectors as the columns of A. Then c1v1+⋯+ckvk=Ac, so:
The columns of A are linearly independent ⟺ Ac=0 has only the trivial solution ⟺ every column of A is a pivot column (no free variables).

Are v1=(1,2,3), v2=(4,5,6), v3=(7,8,9) independent? Row reduce
(147258369)→(1470−3−60−6−12)→(1470−3−6000).
Column 3 is not a pivot column, so the vectors are dependent. The free variable c3=1 gives −3c2−6=0, so c2=−2, and c1+4(−2)+7=0, so c1=1. The dependence relation is
v1−2v2+v3=0.
Check: (1−8+7, 2−10+8, 3−12+9)=(0,0,0). Geometrically, the three vectors lie in one plane through the origin, so their span is that plane, not all of R3.

Theorem.
Any set containing 0 is dependent (1⋅0=0 is a nontrivial relation).
Two vectors are dependent if and only if one is a scalar multiple of the other.
A set of vectors is dependent if and only if at least one of them is a linear combination of the others.
More than n vectors in Rn are always dependent.
Proof of 3. If c1v1+⋯+ckvk=0 with some cj≠0, divide by cj and solve for vj in terms of the others. Conversely, if vj=∑i≠jdivi, then ∑i≠jdivi−vj=0 is a relation with weight −1≠0 on vj. Statement 2 is the case k=2.
Proof of 4. With k>n vectors as columns, A is n×k with more unknowns than equations, so by the Chapter 7 theorem Ac=0 has a nontrivial solution. ■
Watch out: statement 3 says some vector is a combination of the others, not every vector. In {(1,0),(2,0),(0,1)} the first two are dependent, but (0,1) is not a combination of them.
Linear Algebra 02 makes independence and span precise in any vector space and combines them into the idea of a basis.

Is b=(3,1,2) in the span of v1=(1,0,1) and v2=(1,1,0)? If yes, give the weights.
Solution
Solve x(1,0,1)+y(1,1,0)=(3,1,2): the equations are x+y=3, y=1, x=2. They agree: x=2, y=1. So b=2v1+v2, and b is in the span. (Three equations, two unknowns: consistency was not guaranteed; with b=(3,1,3) it would fail.)

Find a unit vector in the direction of (2,−1,2) and a nonzero vector orthogonal to it.
Solution
The length is 4+1+4=3, so the unit vector is (2/3,−1/3,2/3). Any (a,b,c) with 2a−b+2c=0 is orthogonal, for example (1,2,0): 2−2+0=0.

Solve by Gaussian elimination and back substitution: x+y+z=6, 2x+3y+z=11, x+2y+3z=14.
Solution
R2←R2−2R1 gives (0,1,−1∣−1). R3←R3−R1 gives (0,1,2∣8). R3←R3−R2 gives (0,0,3∣9). Back substitution: z=3; y−3=−1 so y=2; x+2+3=6 so x=1. Pivots 1,1,3. Check: 2+6+3=11 and 1+4+9=14.

Bring (1−1232−258) to RREF and write the solution set in parametric vector form.
Solution
R2←R2−2R1 gives (0,0,1∣2). Then R1←R1−2R2 gives (1,−1,0∣−1). Pivot columns 1 and 3; x2=s is free. So x1=−1+s, x3=2:
x=(−102)+s(110).
A line in R3 that does not pass through the origin.

For which h is the system x+2y=4, 3x+6y=h consistent? How many solutions does it have then?
Solution
R2←R2−3R1 gives (0,0∣h−12). Consistent exactly when h=12. Then y is free and there are infinitely many solutions, x=4−2y. In the row picture the two lines are parallel, and they coincide only when h=12.

Are (1,1,0), (0,1,1), (1,0,1) linearly independent? What is their span?
Solution
Row reduce the matrix with these columns: (101110011)→(10101−1011)→(10101−1002). Three pivots, so the columns are independent. Every row has a pivot too, so Ax=b is solvable for every b: the span is all of R3.

Prove: if u and v both solve Ax=0, then so does every linear combination cu+dv. Does the same hold for Ax=b with b≠0?
Solution
A(cu+dv)=cAu+dAv=c0+d0=0. For b≠0 it fails: A(cu+dv)=(c+d)b, which equals b only when c+d=1. (Combinations with weights summing to 1 are called affine combinations; they are exactly what the Chapter 4 proof used.)

Linear Algebra 01 treats matrices as objects in their own right. It multiplies them four different ways, explains why AB≠BA, writes each row operation as an elementary matrix, defines the inverse and computes it by Gauss–Jordan, lists the first equivalent conditions for invertibility, and turns the elimination in Chapter 5 into the factorization A=LU — the form in which every serious linear solver actually works.
